record.title: Enterprise AI Explained: What Leaders Need to Know Beyond Models and Agents
record.subtitle: A plain-language guide to the data, knowledge, models, agents, connections, controls, people and operating decisions that make AI useful in real business work.
record.content_html:
Suppose a service team wants an AI assistant to answer technical questions and prepare customer cases. A demonstration works well: an employee asks a question, the system finds a document and produces a plausible response. The difficult questions arrive the next morning. Which document version can it trust? Does the employee have permission to see the answer? What happens if the system suggests a repair that is wrong, or the connection to the case-management application fails?

This is where enterprise AI becomes a leadership problem. The model matters, but so do the quality of the information, the design of the work, the permissions for using tools, the people who review exceptions and the team that keeps the service running. My starting point is to name the business outcome and its owner, then work backwards through the capabilities needed to deliver it reliably. I would rather operate one narrow, dependable workflow than launch a technically impressive service whose boundaries nobody can explain.

An “Enterprise AI Periodic Table” credited to Prashant Rathi collects 60 terms spanning data, retrieval, models, agents, connections, security and operations. It is a useful map of the vocabulary. It is not a reference architecture or a requirement to buy 60 components. The practical task is to understand which pieces solve a real problem, which are optional and who owns the gaps between them.

Start with the work, then decide what the technology needs

Before discussing models or agents, write a short description of the work in everyday language. Who performs it today? What information do they use? What decision or action follows? What is the baseline for time, quality, risk and cost? Where are delays created by policy, approvals or poor data rather than by a lack of AI? If a broken process is automated unchanged, the organization may simply move its problems faster.

For a customer-service assistant, the goal might be to help an adviser locate the correct procedure and draft a response while leaving final customer communication with the adviser. That description already sets useful boundaries. The system needs reliable, permitted documents and a way to display its source. It may need a connection to a case system, but not permission to close cases, change customer records or order parts. An autonomous agent would add complexity before the business case had justified it.

In my enterprise AI and data leadership work, I have led efforts to give AI initiatives clearer portfolio visibility, assessment criteria and governance foundations, alongside work on data ownership and adoption. The value of that discipline is practical: a proposal can be reviewed as a change to work with measurable conditions, rather than as a request for a fashionable technology. Specialists still decide the detailed technical design; leaders must make the purpose, authority and operating responsibilities explicit.

A useful one-page intake should record the workflow and user group; the intended decision or task; existing baseline; data owner; business process owner; technical service owner; permitted actions; human review points; risk classification; estimated operating cost; and the evidence needed for continuation. If an initiative cannot answer most of these questions, another architecture workshop will not solve the underlying ambiguity.

The eight capability families, explained in business language

1. Data and knowledge: can the system rely on what it receives?

Data foundation covers the information and access needed for the task. Data quality asks whether the records are correct, sufficiently complete, current and fit for the decision. Data lineage shows where a fact came from and how it changed. Metadata describes an asset—its source, owner, date, version or classification. A semantic layer gives consistent business meaning to terms such as “active customer” or “resolved case”. An ontology defines the concepts and relationships in a domain. These last two can be valuable in complicated environments, but most projects should not begin by designing an enterprise-wide ontology.

Knowledge retrieval is a related but different task. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) fetches relevant material before a model writes an answer. Keyword search finds exact terms; vector search finds material with similar meaning; hybrid search combines approaches; reranking reorders candidate results; knowledge graphs connect entities and relationships; GraphRAG uses graph structures in some retrieval-and-reasoning designs. None of these methods independently proves that a retrieved document is correct or that a user should see it.

For a policy assistant, I would first ask who publishes the approved policy, how versions are retired, what the employee may access and how disputes are resolved. Only then would I compare retrieval methods against a representative set of difficult questions. The business failure to avoid is a polished answer based on the wrong document. A simpler search with authoritative sources and visible citations may serve the work better than an elaborate graph system.

2. Models and inference: what kind of intelligence is actually required?

A large language model (LLM) produces or interprets language. A multimodal model can work across formats such as text, images and audio, depending on the product and task. Inference is the act of running a model to produce an output. Fine-tuning adapts some models for a narrower task, while model routing directs requests to different models based on cost, policy, availability or required capability. An AI gateway can centralize approved access, controls and usage visibility.

A model should be selected against the task, not against an abstract leaderboard. A straightforward classification or draft may run adequately on a smaller, less costly model. A difficult reasoning task may require a more capable option, greater review or both. Sometimes established analytics, rules or conventional machine learning are the better choice: forecasting warranty demand does not automatically require a generative model. Fine-tuning should follow a demonstrated gap that cannot be solved more simply through better information, instructions or workflow design.

3. Agents and orchestration: when should AI be allowed to act?

An AI agent is a system that can choose or perform steps toward a goal, usually by interacting with models and tools. Planning breaks an objective into steps; tool selection determines which approved capability to use; orchestration controls their sequence, inputs, retries and state. A multi-agent design divides work between cooperating agents. Human-in-the-loop introduces a human checkpoint for specified decisions. These are design choices, not signs that one solution is inherently more mature than another.

Consider three levels of authority. An assistant suggests an answer; an assisted workflow prepares an action and asks a person to approve it; an agent takes an action within defined limits. Each step increases the need for identity, explicit permission, exception handling and evidence of what happened. I would not give a service assistant the ability to change a customer case just because it can call the relevant API. Approval should follow evidence that autonomous action is safer or more valuable than the narrower alternative.

4. Connectivity and tools: how does AI reach the business systems?

APIs let software exchange requests and results. Connectors provide packaged access to specific services, and webhooks signal that an event occurred. Function calling lets a model-based application request an approved operation through controlled application code. MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes ways AI applications can discover and use exposed tools and resources; A2A (Agent2Agent) is designed for communication between agent systems. These protocols address different forms of connectivity; they do not grant business permission by themselves. The security and authorization design remains a separate responsibility.

Connections need owners and contracts: what can be read, written or deleted; which identity is used; what validation happens before an action; how failures appear; and what is logged. The safest first design often separates a read-only assistant from the transactional system. If a later phase introduces write access, that should trigger a new authorization decision, not happen quietly through a configuration change.

5. Context, memory and state: what should the system remember?

Context engineering chooses which instructions, facts and tools are presented to the model for a particular task. Working memory holds information useful for the current step; session memory maintains continuity during an interaction; long-term memory retains selected information across interactions. State management records where a workflow is, and checkpoints let it resume after an interruption. These are not interchangeable and, in some systems, the “memory” is simply an application database rather than a model feature.

Memory makes services more useful, but keeping information longer also creates privacy, accuracy and retention duties. A customer adviser may need the current case history while drafting a response. That does not automatically justify creating a permanent personal profile of the customer or carrying sensitive details into unrelated conversations. Decide what can be remembered, who may retrieve it, when it expires and how it is corrected or deleted.

6. Security and guardrails: what is the system permitted to do?

Identity establishes who or what is calling the system. Access control limits the data and functions available to that identity. Least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary for the task. Guardrails enforce specific constraints on inputs, outputs and actions, while sandboxing isolates untrusted execution. Prompt-injection defenses try to prevent malicious instructions embedded in documents, messages or tool responses from changing the system’s behavior. They reduce risk but do not make an AI system immune to manipulation.

Security must cover the whole workflow: source documents, user permissions, external tools, output validation, secrets, logs and downstream applications. The OWASP guidance for LLM applications identifies issues including prompt injection, sensitive-information disclosure and excessive agency. For a business leader, the practical question is straightforward: if an untrusted document tells the assistant to ignore its rules or send data elsewhere, which technical controls and permission boundaries prevent that request from becoming an action?

7. Evaluation and operations: how will we know it keeps working?

Evaluation tests the quality and safety of answers against representative tasks. Metrics track outcomes such as correct completion, error and escalation rates, latency and operating cost. Logging records significant inputs, actions and outputs within approved privacy limits; tracing follows a request across components. Drift detection looks for changes in data or performance, and feedback loops support correction. LLMOps covers the ongoing work of testing, releasing, monitoring and maintaining model-based applications.

Reliability also depends on ordinary engineering practices. Timeouts stop stalled operations; retries attempt temporary failures again; circuit breakers prevent repeated calls to failing services; fallback routes provide an alternative; autoscaling adjusts resources to demand. These mechanisms should be designed for the consequences of the business action. Retrying a document lookup is different from retrying a payment or duplicate customer update. A failed workflow needs a safe state, a clear owner and a way to recover without repeating harmful actions.

8. Governance, cost and adoption: who owns the result?

Responsible AI concerns the suitability and consequences of a use case, including fairness, privacy, safety and transparency. AI governance sets the policies, decision rights and oversight needed to apply those principles. Auditability records what was approved, which system version acted and who resolved an exception. Cost control covers model usage, infrastructure, data pipelines, service support and people’s time. AI ROI is the business case tested against actual costs and outcomes, rather than a count of prompts or licences.

Adoption means people can use the capability appropriately in the work that matters. Training attendance alone cannot prove that. I would look for observed task completion, the need for rework, correct challenges to bad recommendations, user confidence grounded in experience and the burden transferred to other teams. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its generative-AI profile offer useful external references for managing risks across a system’s life cycle. They do not replace a local owner’s decision about what is acceptable in a particular workflow.

Three operating designs—and when not to buy more complexity

Pattern A: Find and explain. An employee asks a question; the application searches approved knowledge; a model drafts an answer with sources; the employee decides what to do. The main work is source ownership, retrieval quality, permissions and answer evaluation. This pattern may need no agent, long-term memory, knowledge graph or fine-tuning.

Pattern B: Prepare and approve. The system reads permitted records, assembles a draft case or recommendation and presents it for human approval. It now needs clear workflow state, a durable record of what the reviewer saw and controls preventing approval from being bypassed. A reliable deterministic workflow with occasional model calls may be preferable to a free-form agent.

Pattern C: Act within limits. An agent selects tools and carries out a bounded action, such as creating a draft task or updating an approved low-risk field. This requires stronger identity, least-privilege access, action validation, transaction safeguards, recovery, monitoring and named operational ownership. Multi-agent coordination, A2A or more persistent memory should be added only if a defined problem justifies their cost and risk.

These are design patterns, not a ladder every organization must climb. An excellent read-only assistant can be a finished product. Autonomy is justified by business value and reliable evidence, not by a desire to display the latest technical capabilities.

A worked example: moving a service assistant into everyday operations

Illustrative scenario, not a claim about a particular employer or deployed system. A service organization receives recurring technical questions from advisers. It wants to reduce searching time while preserving the quality of guidance. The first proposal includes a large model, vector search, multi-agent orchestration and the ability to update cases. A useful design review starts by asking which of these parts the task actually requires.

First, restrict the problem. Choose one defined group of advisers and one approved knowledge collection. Establish who owns the documents and which versions are valid. Identify a baseline using a sample of real tasks, anonymized and handled under the organization’s data rules. Record time spent searching, whether the right answer was found, how often escalation was needed and whether final advice was correct.

Second, build the narrowest service that could help. Try approved enterprise search plus a model that cites its sources. Test exact-phrase and meaning-based retrieval; introduce hybrid search or reranking only where tests show a material benefit. Keep the model from updating the case system. The adviser remains responsible for the decision and can see when evidence is missing or conflicting.

Third, challenge it deliberately. Test outdated procedures, ambiguous product variants, contradictory documents, questions beyond permission, prompt-injection attempts, system downtime and low-confidence answers. Evaluate the whole user task, not merely whether the model sounds convincing. A correct answer delivered too late, without an accessible citation or to the wrong employee is not a reliable service outcome.

Fourth, establish the operating contract. Name the business owner for the service outcome, the knowledge owner for content, the technical owner for availability and security, and the person who can suspend use. Decide how updates are reviewed, which incidents require escalation and how users report wrong answers. Start with limited use and a scheduled evidence review. The case for expanding to another team must include local knowledge differences and changed-work measures, not just successful demonstrations.

Only then consider more authority. If the assistant reliably drafts a case update, a human-approval step may justify adding the relevant API. Fully automatic case changes would require a new risk decision and stronger recovery evidence. This staged approach limits avoidable expense while protecting the option to expand later.

How to keep an enterprise AI service affordable

Production cost is broader than tokens. A useful budget covers model calls, retrieval and indexing, hosting, connectors, security testing, monitoring, support, content stewardship, training and the time people spend reviewing outputs. An inexpensive model that creates heavy rework can cost more than a capable one; the reverse is also possible. The meaningful unit is cost per correctly completed business task, including exceptions—not cost per prompt alone.

Start with technology the organization already has permission and capacity to operate. Use a smaller or less expensive model for routine requests when evaluation supports it; route only the harder tasks to a stronger one. Set usage quotas and limits, watch unnecessary repeated calls, restrict retrieval to relevant sources and measure whether caching is appropriate and safe. Retain a simple rule-based step where it works. Avoid premature fine-tuning, broad persistent memory and multi-agent designs until their incremental value has been demonstrated.

Be equally careful with spending outside the model. Someone must maintain source documents and access rules. Connectors need testing when enterprise applications change. A help desk needs a clear route for defects. If those tasks have no funded owner, the model invoice may look reasonable while the real operating bill remains invisible. I would fund the minimum dependable service first, then buy more capability against evidence of improved outcomes.

A 30–60–90-day leadership plan

Days 1–30: choose and define. Select one meaningful workflow and one accountable sponsor. Agree the baseline, task boundary, user group and expected benefit. Review source quality, access permissions, legal/security requirements, existing platforms and the current process. Identify the smallest technical pattern that could meet the need. The output should be a one-page service charter and an evaluation set drawn from realistic tasks.

Days 31–60: test the full task. Build or configure a bounded service. Compare model and retrieval options on the same examples, including difficult and unsafe cases. Test failure and recovery, log essential events within privacy rules and measure the full cost of a completed task. Have real practitioners challenge the output and report where the workflow still fails. End this phase with evidence for continuing, changing design or stopping—not a slide claiming success because the demo ran.

Days 61–90: operate on a limited scale. Introduce the service to a defined group with documented permissions, support ownership, escalation paths and a change process. Compare actual outcomes with the original baseline, including quality, rework, exceptions and time saved where attributable. Decide whether to continue, expand, adapt or stop. Expansion should be treated as a fresh receiving-team review, because another unit may have different data, rules and skill levels.

Before authorizing wider use, ask ten questions:

  1. Which measurable business task improves, and what is today’s baseline?
  2. Who owns the outcome when the project team leaves?
  3. Which data and documents are authoritative, current and permitted for this user?
  4. Why is AI needed here, rather than simpler search, analytics or process redesign?
  5. What can the system advise, draft, approve or execute—and what is forbidden?
  6. What happens when the model, tool, document or network fails?
  7. How will we test incorrect, unsafe, ambiguous and unauthorized outputs?
  8. What does one correctly completed task cost, including review and support?
  9. Can employees challenge results, and does the workflow make that practical?
  10. What evidence will justify expansion, modification or shutdown?

Those answers form a better executive release discussion than a list of model names. The technical team can still choose sophisticated components where they are needed. Leadership provides the conditions that allow those components to deliver something stable and useful.

Reading the 60 concepts without getting lost in them

The infographic that prompted this article mixes capabilities (such as retrieval), techniques (such as reranking), technical interfaces (such as APIs and MCP), operating safeguards (such as retries and circuit breakers) and management responsibilities (such as governance and adoption). That mix explains why the field can feel overwhelming. A periodic table makes the names memorable; it does not tell a leader which choices are mandatory or in what order they should be made.

I would group the terms into four practical questions: What must the system know? (data, metadata, knowledge, retrieval and context); What must it produce or do? (models, inference, planning, agents and tools); What constrains and sustains it? (identity, permissions, security, evaluation, logs and reliability); and Who decides whether it is worthwhile? (process owners, governance, adoption, cost and business outcomes). The categories are meant to help leaders hold the right conversation, not to prescribe one technology stack.

There is a healthy counterargument to building too much structure: heavy governance and infrastructure can consume the resources needed to learn from a small trial. I agree that early experimentation should remain proportionate. The answer is to make permission, data boundaries, business ownership and a few outcome tests clear from the start, then deepen the controls as risk, integration and autonomy increase. Small experiments need clarity; high-consequence systems need stronger proof.

The decision I would take into the next AI steering meeting is simple: choose one real workflow, name its owner and ask the team to show the minimum system that can complete it safely. If that system improves work at an acceptable total cost, extend it deliberately. If it cannot, another layer of AI architecture is unlikely to fix the business decision that was left unresolved.

Sources and further reading: Concepts prompted by the user-supplied “Enterprise AI Periodic Table” credited to Prashant Rathi (used as inspiration, not reproduced); NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile; OWASP LLM application risks; MCP specification; and A2A protocol specification. The worked service case is illustrative; proposed checks are managerial recommendations, not measured results from that example.
record.excerpt: Enterprise AI is a connected business system, not a shopping list of 60 technologies. Start with one workflow and a named owner, then decide which data, models, tools, safeguards and support it genuinely needs. This guide explains the choices, the costs and the evidence leaders should require before scaling.
